He told the gathering, "I've thought a lot about it, but at the end of Desert Storm, the question was should we have kind of kept going on that road to death and all this slaughter until Saddam Hussein showed up and laid his sword on the table, surrendered. Bush recalled their talk, "I said, 'What if we just say he has to come to surrender, would he have done it?' And this guy said, 'I'm absolutely convinced he would have.' My experts tell me he wouldn't have." Bush said, "We ended it the way we said we would" as a military success, but noted a cleaner ending "would have been perfect." He added, "If we had tried to get Saddam Hussein to come and literally surrender and put his sword on the table, I think it might have been avoided some of the problems that we did have in the future from him." On a day that President Barack Obama dispatched George Mitchell to the Middle East as the latest U.S. envoy, Clinton discussed the failure to achieve peace between Israelis and Palestinians. "My No. 1 regret is that I was not able to persuade Yasser Arafat to accept the peace plan I offered at the end of my presidency that the Israelis accepted. "If he had done that ... we had had seven years of progress toward peace. We had one year in 1998, the only year in the history of Israel where not a single soul was killed in a terrorist act. The Palestinians had more control over West Bank then than they do today," Clinton said. "And if he had taken that deal, we would have a Palestinian state and we would have had, I think now, normal peaceful relations with Israel and all of its Arab neighbors." Clinton said a deal would have helped the U.S. handle other issues in the region, saying, "We'd be much better positioned to deal with the problem of Iran, and we would have taken away about half the arguments of terrorists around the world by giving the Palestinians their state and creating a cooperative, positive interdependence in the Middle East, not a negative one. And so, I think that would have done more good to save more lives and help more people, and I wish I had been able to do that. " Clinton also said he regretted not doing more to "stop the Rwandan genocide," and succeeding on a new health care plan. He said "presidents should share freely ... the mistakes they made" with historians, because it teaches lessons. He said he shared problems during the lunch with Obama and the four living presidents, saying, "You want each new president to make new mistakes, not the same ones." Clinton added, "all of us know if you make enough decisions, you're going to make a few of them aren't right."

(CNN) — Two former presidents reflected Monday on their greatest regrets in office, each revisiting issues that continue to trouble the nation years later.

Former presidents and political rivals Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush, who now share philanthropic efforts, appeared together at a question-and-answer forum before the National Automobile Dealers Association in New Orleans, Louisiana.

Asked about his biggest regret after leaving office, Bush said he now wonders whether he should have tried to force Saddam Hussein from power at the end of the first Gulf War in 1991.

“I’ve thought a lot about it,” he told the gathering, “but at the end of Desert Storm, the question was: should we have kind of kept going on that road to death and all this slaughter until Saddam Hussein showed up and laid his sword on the table, surrendered? And the common wisdom was he wouldn’t do that.”

But Bush said a conversation with an FBI agent who interrogated Saddam after his capture has prompted him to reconsider.

“I said, ‘What if we just say he has to come to surrender, would he have done it?’ And this guy said, ‘I’m absolutely convinced he would have.’ My experts tell me he wouldn’t have,” Bush recalled.

Bush said, “We ended it the way we said we would” as a military success, but noted that a cleaner ending “would have been perfect.”

He added, “If we had tried to get Saddam Hussein to come and literally surrender and put his sword on the table, I think it might have avoided some of the problems that we did have in the future from him.”

On a day when President Barack Obama dispatched George Mitchell to the Middle East as the latest U.S. envoy, Clinton discussed the failure to achieve peace between Israelis and Palestinians.

“My No. 1 regret is that I was not able to persuade Yasser Arafat to accept the peace plan I offered at the end of my presidency that the Israelis accepted,” Clinton said.

“If he had done that ... we had had seven years of progress toward peace. We had one year in 1998, the only year in the history of Israel where not a single soul was killed in a terrorist act. The Palestinians had more control over the West Bank then than they do today,” Clinton said.

“And if he had taken that deal, we would have a Palestinian state and we would have had, I think now, normal peaceful relations with Israel and all of its Arab neighbors.”

Clinton said such an agreement would have helped the United States address other issues in the region.

“We’d be much better positioned to deal with the problem of Iran, and we would have taken away about half the arguments of terrorists around the world by giving the Palestinians their state and creating a cooperative, positive interdependence in the Middle East, not a negative one,” he said. “And so, I think that would have done more good to save more lives and help more people, and I wish I had been able to do that.”

Clinton also said he regretted not doing more to “stop the Rwandan genocide” and not succeeding in passing a new health care plan.

He said “presidents should share freely ... the mistakes they made” with historians because doing so teaches valuable lessons. Clinton said he shared such reflections during a lunch with Obama and the four living presidents, adding, “You want each new president to make new mistakes, not the same ones.”

Clinton added, “All of us know if you make enough decisions, you’re going to make a few of them that aren’t right.”

(CNN) — On Monday, two former U.S. presidents spoke about the decisions they most wish had turned out differently while they were in office, pointing to problems that were still troubling the country years afterward.

Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush, once political opponents, have since worked together on charitable initiatives. The two former presidents appeared side by side at a question-and-answer event hosted by the National Automobile Dealers Association in New Orleans, Louisiana.

When asked about his greatest regret after leaving the presidency, Bush said he has since questioned whether he should have pushed harder for Saddam Hussein to be removed from power at the conclusion of the first Gulf War in 1991.

Bush told the audience that he has spent a great deal of time thinking about the issue. At the close of Desert Storm, he said, the question was whether U.S.-led forces should have continued “on that road to death and all this slaughter” until Saddam appeared, placed his sword on the table and surrendered. At the time, Bush said, the general belief was that Saddam would never do that.

However, Bush said a later discussion with an FBI agent who questioned Saddam after his capture caused him to rethink the matter. Bush said he asked the agent whether Saddam would have surrendered if the demand had simply been made. According to Bush, the agent replied that he was “absolutely convinced” Saddam would have done so, even though Bush’s own advisers had told him otherwise.

Bush said the war was brought to a close in the way the United States had promised and described it as a military success. Still, he said a more decisive conclusion “would have been perfect.” He added that if the United States had attempted to make Saddam personally surrender and symbolically lay down his sword, some later problems caused by Saddam might have been avoided.

That same day, President Barack Obama sent George Mitchell to the Middle East as the newest U.S. envoy. Clinton, meanwhile, spoke about his disappointment over failing to secure peace between Israelis and Palestinians.

Clinton said his top regret was that he could not convince Yasser Arafat to accept the peace proposal he put forward near the end of his presidency, a plan that he said the Israelis had agreed to.

According to Clinton, the region had experienced seven years of movement toward peace. He noted that in 1998, for the only year in Israel’s history, no one was killed in a terrorist attack. He also said Palestinians then had greater authority over the West Bank than they have today.

Clinton said that if Arafat had accepted the agreement, there would have been a Palestinian state, and he believed Israel and all of its Arab neighbors would by then have had normal, peaceful relations.

He also argued that such an agreement would have improved the United States’ ability to address other challenges in the region. Clinton said the U.S. would have been in a stronger position to deal with Iran and that granting Palestinians a state would have removed roughly half of the arguments used by terrorists around the world. He said the deal could have created a constructive and cooperative interdependence in the Middle East rather than a harmful one. For that reason, Clinton said, it would have saved more lives, helped more people and done more good, and he wished he had been able to achieve it.

Clinton also said he regretted not doing more to stop the genocide in Rwanda and not succeeding in passing a new health care plan.

He said presidents should be open with historians about the mistakes they made because those mistakes offer lessons. Clinton said he had discussed such problems during a lunch with Obama and the four living former presidents, explaining that each new president should make different mistakes rather than repeat old ones.

Clinton added that anyone who makes enough decisions will inevitably make some that turn out to be wrong.

**Clinton, George H.W. Bush reflect on biggest presidential regrets at New Orleans forum**

**NEW ORLEANS** — Two former presidents from opposing political parties shared a stage Saturday and offered a rare, candid look at the burdens of the Oval Office, including the decisions they still wish had gone differently.

Appearing at a National Automobile Dealers Association forum in New Orleans, former Presidents Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush spoke about leadership, bipartisanship and the weight of presidential decision-making before an audience of auto dealers and industry leaders.

Clinton said one of his deepest regrets from his time in office was the United States’ failure to intervene more forcefully during the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, where hundreds of thousands of people were killed in a matter of months.

“I think about Rwanda,” Clinton said, reflecting on the limits and consequences of American action abroad. He has previously called the episode one of the greatest failures of his presidency.

Bush, who served as the 41st president from 1989 to 1993, pointed to the political fallout from his decision to break his “no new taxes” pledge as one of the most difficult moments of his presidency. The move, part of a 1990 budget deal with Democrats, helped reduce the deficit but damaged his standing with conservatives and followed him into his unsuccessful 1992 reelection campaign.

The conversation brought together two men once divided by a hard-fought presidential contest. Clinton defeated Bush in 1992, ending the Republican president’s bid for a second term. But in the years that followed, the two developed a well-known friendship, working together on disaster relief efforts and often speaking warmly of one another in public.

Their appearance in New Orleans underscored that unlikely bond.

Both men emphasized that presidents often face decisions with incomplete information and long-term consequences that are not always clear in the moment. They also spoke about the importance of compromise — a theme that drew attention at a time of sharp partisan divisions in Washington.

The forum was part of the National Automobile Dealers Association’s annual gathering, which regularly features political figures, business leaders and public officials addressing economic and industry issues.

**Bush and Clinton Reflect on Iraq, Saddam Hussein, Middle East Peace, Rwanda and Health Care in Rare Joint Appearance**

**By Staff Writer**

In a rare joint appearance that blended foreign-policy reflection with flashes of bipartisan warmth, former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton revisited some of the most consequential decisions of their presidencies, offering sharply different but often complementary perspectives on Iraq, Saddam Hussein, Middle East peace, the Rwandan genocide and the long-running struggle over health care in the United States.

The two former presidents, appearing together before a large audience of civic leaders, students and policy experts, spoke less as political rivals than as veterans of the presidency weighing the burdens of power. Their conversation underscored how decisions made in the Oval Office can echo for decades — shaping wars, humanitarian crises, diplomatic openings and domestic debates that remain unresolved.

Bush, the 41st president, returned repeatedly to the 1991 Gulf War, defending his administration’s decision to build a broad international coalition to expel Saddam Hussein’s forces from Kuwait while stopping short of marching on Baghdad. Clinton, the 42nd president, reflected on the challenge of containing Saddam during the 1990s, the frustration of failed peace efforts in the Middle East, the moral stain of Rwanda and the political difficulty of reforming American health care.

The appearance offered a striking contrast in style: Bush, measured and rooted in the language of alliance management and restraint; Clinton, expansive and analytical, often moving from historical detail to broader lessons about political leadership.

### Iraq and the Decision Not to Remove Saddam Hussein

Bush described the Gulf War as a defining test of the post-Cold War international order. Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait in August 1990, he said, demanded a response not only because of Kuwait’s sovereignty but because unchecked aggression could destabilize the broader Middle East.

He emphasized that the success of the war depended on international legitimacy. His administration secured United Nations resolutions, assembled a coalition that included Arab states, and maintained clear military objectives: drive Iraqi forces out of Kuwait and restore the Kuwaiti government.

The former president defended the decision not to pursue Saddam Hussein’s regime into Baghdad after Iraqi forces were defeated.

According to Bush, expanding the mission would have fractured the coalition, risked a long occupation and left the United States responsible for governing Iraq without a clear exit strategy. He argued that restraint was not weakness but a recognition of the limits of military power.

Clinton, who inherited the Iraq problem when he took office in 1993, said his administration faced a different challenge: not liberating Kuwait, but containing Saddam through sanctions, weapons inspections and periodic military pressure. He recalled that Saddam repeatedly tested international resolve, especially over weapons inspections and compliance with U.N. demands.

Clinton noted that Iraq remained a persistent security concern throughout his presidency, citing confrontations over weapons inspections and U.S. strikes ordered in response to Iraqi defiance. But he also suggested that the experience showed how difficult it is to manage a hostile regime through containment alone.

Both men spoke of Saddam Hussein as a brutal dictator who inflicted enormous suffering on Iraqis and threatened his neighbors. Yet both also acknowledged the complexity of translating opposition to a dictator into a sustainable policy for the region.

### Saddam Hussein and the Limits of American Power

The discussion of Saddam opened into a broader meditation on American power. Bush argued that military action is most effective when objectives are limited, alliances are strong and the public understands the mission. Clinton agreed that presidents must consider not only whether the United States can win a military conflict, but what follows afterward.

Clinton said the central question in dealing with dictators is often not whether they are morally reprehensible, but whether the United States has a viable strategy to change their behavior or replace them without creating greater instability.

The two former presidents did not dwell directly on later U.S. policy in Iraq, but their remarks carried an implicit relevance to the debates that followed the 2003 invasion under President George W. Bush. The elder Bush’s defense of coalition warfare and limited aims stood in contrast to more expansive visions of regime change, while Clinton’s comments reflected the dilemmas of containment and the difficulty of enforcing international norms over time.

### Middle East Peace: Hope, Frustration and Missed Opportunities

Turning to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, Clinton offered some of his most detailed remarks of the appearance. He described the pursuit of Middle East peace as one of the most difficult and emotionally charged efforts of his presidency.

Clinton recalled the optimism surrounding the Oslo process, the handshake between Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, and the belief that a negotiated settlement might be possible. He said Rabin’s assassination in 1995 was a devastating blow, both politically and psychologically, to the peace process.

He also reflected on the 2000 Camp David summit, where his administration sought to broker a final-status agreement between Israel and the Palestinians. Clinton said the talks came closer than many people realized but ultimately failed because the gaps on territory, Jerusalem, refugees and security remained too deep.

Bush, whose administration convened the 1991 Madrid Peace Conference after the Gulf War, said that American credibility in the region depends on persistence, fairness and close coordination with allies. He characterized Madrid as an important opening that brought Israelis and Arab representatives into direct talks, even if it did not produce an immediate settlement.

Both former presidents expressed concern that the promise of a two-state solution had become harder to realize over time. They pointed to distrust, violence, political fragmentation and the absence of sustained leadership as barriers to peace.

Clinton argued that peace efforts require leaders on both sides who are willing to risk political capital. Bush added that American presidents can encourage and facilitate negotiations, but they cannot impose peace if the parties themselves are not prepared to make painful compromises.

### Rwanda and the Burden of Inaction

One of the most somber portions of the event came when Clinton addressed Rwanda, where an estimated 800,000 people were killed in 1994 during a genocide carried out against Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Clinton has previously called the failure to intervene one of the greatest regrets of his presidency, and he returned to that theme during the discussion. He said the United States and the international community did not act with the urgency the crisis demanded.

The former president acknowledged that officials at the time were influenced by the recent deaths of American soldiers in Somalia and by reluctance to commit forces to another African conflict. But he said those explanations do not erase the moral failure.

Bush, who had left office before the genocide, spoke more broadly about the difficulty presidents face in identifying humanitarian crises early and mobilizing public and international support before mass killing accelerates. He said Rwanda remains a warning about the cost of indifference and the danger of assuming that atrocities in smaller or poorer countries will remain strategically irrelevant.

Clinton said Rwanda reshaped his thinking about humanitarian intervention, influencing later decisions in the Balkans, where NATO intervened in Bosnia and Kosovo during his presidency. He suggested that the lesson of Rwanda is that the world needs better mechanisms to detect, prevent and respond to mass atrocities before they become genocides.

### Health Care and the Politics of Reform

The conversation then shifted from foreign policy to domestic affairs, with Clinton discussing the failed health care reform effort led by his administration in 1993 and 1994.

Clinton said the attempt to overhaul the health care system was driven by real problems: rising costs, uneven coverage and fear among working families that illness could lead to financial ruin. But he acknowledged that the proposal became politically vulnerable because of its complexity, the scale of the change it proposed and the strength of opposition from industry groups and Republicans.

He said one lesson of the failed effort was that health care reform requires not only policy design but public trust. Americans needed to understand how reforms would affect their doctors, employers, premiums and choices, he said, and his administration did not succeed in communicating that clearly enough.

Bush, who opposed major government expansion in health care during his presidency, framed the issue in terms of balancing access, affordability and market forces. He said presidents must be cautious about promising sweeping reforms in a system that touches every household and a large share of the economy.

Despite their differences, both men agreed that health care has remained a persistent national challenge because it sits at the intersection of economics, medicine, politics and personal anxiety.

Clinton said the continued debate over health care reflected a basic unresolved question: whether the United States should treat health coverage as a universal guarantee, an employment-based benefit, a market commodity or some combination of all three.

### Bipartisanship and the Presidency

Beyond the policy discussions, the appearance was notable for its tone. Bush and Clinton, once rivals across a sharp partisan divide, displayed the personal rapport that developed after Clinton defeated Bush in the 1992 presidential election and later worked with him on humanitarian relief efforts.

Their joint presence served as a reminder of a less common tradition in American politics: former presidents publicly disagreeing on policy while showing respect for one another’s service and burdens.

Both men spoke about the loneliness of presidential decision-making. They said that even with advisers, intelligence briefings and public pressure, the final responsibility rests with the person behind the Resolute Desk.

Bush emphasized prudence, alliances and the importance of knowing the limits of American intervention. Clinton emphasized engagement, adaptability and the need to learn from failure.

Together, their reflections offered a sweeping view of U.S. leadership at the end of the Cold War and the beginning of a more uncertain era — one defined by regional conflicts, humanitarian crises, terrorism, globalization and unresolved domestic reform.

The event ended not with a partisan flourish, but with a shared message: history judges presidents not only by their intentions, but by the consequences of their decisions — including the wars they fight, the wars they avoid, the lives they fail to save and the reforms they leave unfinished.

**Clinton, Bush Share Lessons From Mistakes at Auto Dealers Forum**

Former presidents Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush, once political rivals, offered a bipartisan lesson in leadership and humility during a public forum before the National Automobile Dealers Association, reflecting on mistakes they made in office and the challenges of governing under intense scrutiny.

Appearing together before the trade group, Clinton and Bush spoke candidly about decisions they said they would handle differently if given another chance. The discussion mixed policy reflection with humor, underscoring the cordial relationship the two men developed years after the 1992 presidential campaign, when Clinton defeated Bush’s bid for a second term.

Bush pointed to the difficulty of balancing principle and political reality, including the fallout from his decision to support a budget agreement that included tax increases after his well-known “no new taxes” pledge. He said presidents often face choices in which the best available option still carries political costs.

Clinton, reflecting on his two terms, said one lesson was the importance of understanding public concerns and building broader support before pursuing major initiatives. He has previously cited the failed health care overhaul effort early in his presidency as an example of moving too quickly without enough consensus.

(CNN) -- Former Presidents Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush, reflecting on the burdens of the Oval Office, said their deepest regrets were tied less to politics than to the human consequences of decisions made — or not made — while they held power.

Clinton pointed to the 1994 genocide in Rwanda as the failure that has weighed most heavily on him. During his presidency, extremist Hutu militias slaughtered an estimated 800,000 people, most of them Tutsis, while the United States and much of the international community avoided direct intervention.

“I have a regret that I didn’t do more to try to stop the slaughter in Rwanda,” Clinton has said in reflecting on his presidency. He has often described the episode as one of the clearest moral failures of his time in office, saying the United States might not have been able to prevent all of the killing but could have helped save lives.

The former president has said that, in hindsight, Washington was too cautious after the deaths of American troops in Somalia and too slow to recognize the scale of the unfolding massacre. “I don’t think we could have ended the violence, but I think we could have cut it down,” Clinton has said. “And I regret it.”

Bush, whose presidency was defined by the end of the Cold War, the reunification of Germany and the 1991 Persian Gulf War, has spoken about regret in a different way. He has resisted portraying any one decision as a simple mistake, often emphasizing the limits and trade-offs of presidential leadership.

One of the most politically damaging moments of Bush’s presidency was his decision to agree to a tax increase after famously promising at the 1988 Republican National Convention: “Read my lips: no new taxes.” The reversal helped fracture his conservative support and became a defining issue in his 1992 loss to Clinton.

Bush later defended the budget deal as necessary, even though it hurt him politically. He suggested the decision reflected the difference between campaigning and governing — and the reality that presidents sometimes must absorb political damage in pursuit of what they believe is the national interest.

The reflections from Clinton and Bush came against a broader backdrop of another president confronting the early weight of foreign policy. President Barack Obama, shortly after taking office, moved quickly to signal a renewed U.S. role in Middle East diplomacy by sending former Senate Majority Leader George Mitchell to the region as a special envoy.

Mitchell, who helped broker the Good Friday Agreement in Northern Ireland and later led a fact-finding mission on Israeli-Palestinian violence, was tasked with meeting leaders in the region and exploring ways to revive peace efforts after years of stalled negotiations and renewed conflict.

Obama’s decision to dispatch Mitchell so early underscored the point both former presidents knew well: foreign crises rarely wait for a new administration to settle in. The Middle East, like Rwanda for Clinton and the Gulf for Bush, presented questions of timing, leverage and moral responsibility — the kinds of choices that can define a presidency long after the politics of the moment have faded.

Clinton praised Mitchell’s diplomatic credentials, describing him as a serious and patient negotiator well suited to the region’s complexities. Bush, too, had long experience with Middle East diplomacy, having assembled the international coalition that expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait and having helped convene the 1991 Madrid peace conference.

Together, the reflections offered a rare glimpse into how former presidents measure their own records. Campaign promises, approval ratings and partisan victories may dominate the headlines while a president is in office. But years later, Clinton and Bush suggested, the memories that endure are often the lives affected by decisions made under pressure — and the knowledge that even the most powerful office in the world comes with limits.
